Seasonal Water Yield: preparing global run

Status of tools, data, and Borneo test plan

10 September 2026

Global NCP — SWY Status Memo

Prepared by Jerónimo Rodríguez Escobar Global Science, WWF 10 September 2026

Where we stand

This is a new model run, not a table update. The other InVEST outputs were handed pre-computed; SWY has not been run globally yet, because a single global calibration isn’t feasible. Producing an output means assembling every real input and running the model from scratch.

The orchestration is real and confirmed, not assumed. Rich’s swy_global + inspring were read directly at the code level, not from descriptions: basin batching, per-basin routing, global-mosaic stitching, and direct CN/Kc raster overrides all work as expected. One real bug found in inspring itself along the way (a dead root_depth parameter).

The plan is test-then-scale, decided with Becky 2026-09-09: Borneo — and the first real in-house attempt ran. Quickflow (mean 406.8mm/year) and actual ET (mean 1288.0mm/year) both land in physically plausible ranges for tropical rainforest. One genuine, diagnosable issue found, not hidden: ~4.6% of local-recharge pixels show a flow-accumulation anomaly, likely an unresolved DEM sink — detail below. Meeting with Becky and Rich together today, 2026-09-11.

Question

Is this project’s own CN/Kc parametrization, built from public, peer-reviewed global products robust enough to trust at the global scale.

Running end-to-end on a real study area as check (Borneo).

(A stricter version of this question — does it reproduce a known, published result closely enough to trust scaling further — was the original framing, tested against one of Hamel et al. 2020’s own basins. Kept as a reference in the validation section below; it isn’t blocking this round.)

What the model needs, and where each piece stands

Input Status
AOI / watershed vector Built — borneo_aoi.gpkg, a single dissolved polygon from HydroBASINS Australia/Oceania level-6 units intersecting Borneo, built 2026-09-10 (computed area 753,803 km² vs. real ~743,330 km², 1.4% off)
DEM Sourced and verified — SRTMGL3, 90m, via AppEEARS. Elevation range -91–4041m (Mt. Kinabalu, Borneo’s real high point, is 4095m — a close, correct match)
Routing parameters Found — Rich’s swy_global.ini defaults (THRESHOLD_FLOW_ACCUMULATION=1000, ALPHA_M=0.083333, BETA_I=1, GAMMA=1, MAX_PIXEL_FILL_COUNT=1000000)
LULC Sourced and verified — real 2020 Copernicus C3S land cover, extracted from the user’s WWF OneDrive copy after this project’s local file turned out to be an empty/corrupted stub (a real data-integrity finding, not a download gap). 48.1% valid fraction matches every other Borneo raster; plausible class mix (58.3% broadleaf evergreen forest)
Monthly precipitation Sourced and verified — CHIRPS 2020, ~5.5km, clipped to Borneo. July mean 138.9mm, plausible for the region
Monthly ET0 Sourced and verified — TerraClimate pet (Penman-Monteith, CO2-corrected), ~4km. Monthly means 97–118mm, plausible for tropical reference ET. New source as of 2026-09-10 — CHIRPS is precipitation-only
Soil hydrologic group HYSOGs250m — downloaded 2026-09-09 (global file, data/raw/soil_hydrologic_group/)
Rain events Placeholder used for the first run (uniform 18 events/month) — not derived from real daily CHIRPS. The documented derivation method needs Google Earth Engine access not set up in this environment; a real gap, flagged not hidden
Curve number (CN) GCN250 as global base, confirmed sourced; biome-specific patches not yet applied for this first attempt — see below
Crop coefficient (Kc) NDVI sourced and verified (MOD13A3, full 2000–2026 record; ~0.82 mean for a July granule, plausible for rainforest) and used directly — see below for how
root_depth Required by the interface but confirmed dead in this model fork — satisfied with a placeholder raster, not worth sourcing carefully

Curve number: the harder parameter, and where the gap actually is

InVEST’s own documentation is explicit that there’s no global shortcut for CN — it depends on soil group, cover type, and moisture condition, and region-specific values are preferred over blanket defaults. GCN250 solves the bulk of this: a purpose-built, peer-reviewed global CN product combining land cover and soil hydrologic group. Its own authors are candid that it differentiates by land-cover granularity, not by region-specific values within one land-cover class — and that the underlying method is least validated in forested/humid environments, which is exactly this project’s LAC focus.

Biome Status
Tropical moist broadleaf forest Real candidate literature found (Calero Mosquera et al. 2021, Fábrega et al. 2012) — both directly confirm the standard method overestimates runoff under tropical conditions. Patch is buildable.
Mangroves No usable literature found after three separate search passes. The underlying reason: these are tide-flooded systems — CN’s rainfall-runoff premise doesn’t describe what’s driving water movement here. Leaning toward documenting this as a structural limitation rather than continuing to search.
Flooded grasslands / savannas Same missing-CN-number problem, but a different mechanism: these are river-overflow-flooded (seasonal inundation), not tidal. Same underlying failure mode as mangroves — a flood-pulse-dominated system CN’s premise wasn’t built for — just a different flood driver. The Colombian Llanos is the real, motivated test case for this specifically — sequenced after the basin validation above, not instead of it.

Why this matters more than it might look: in Hamel et al. (2020)’s own sensitivity analysis, quickflow changed by factors of 10–13× between antecedent-moisture CN settings in one basin. CN is close to the dominant source of variance in this model’s output, not a minor calibration knob.

A real architectural finding, from 2026-09-10: inspring’s SWY implementation accepts CN as a direct raster override (cn_a/b/c/d_path), not only via a lucode-indexed biophysical table. Since GCN250 is already a per-pixel product, that’s the architecturally better long-term path — not a novel idea on our part; continuous, gridded parameterization is the norm for physically-based hydrology models generally, and InVEST’s table-based convention is a design choice suited to its usual land-use-scenario use case. For this first run attempt, the simpler CSV table path was used instead (built from GCN250’s own crosswalk, no biome patches applied yet) — lower-risk for a first pass; the raster-override path is worth a follow-up round.

Crop coefficient: mostly solved by NDVI, not a table

  • Cropland: the plan is standard FAO-56 values with region-correct crop-calendar timing (real remaining work — the available reference spreadsheet’s defaults are Northern-Hemisphere only, and oil palm, likely Borneo’s dominant cropland, isn’t a native FAO-56 entry).
  • Everything else (forest, grassland, shrubland — most of global land area): no table needed. A validated NDVI regression (Kamble et al. 2013, corroborated by multiple follow-up studies through 2025) computes Kc directly per pixel per month from satellite NDVI.
  • Non-vegetated (water, wetlands, bare soil, built): fixed values from InVEST’s own guidance.
  • For this first run attempt: the NDVI regression was applied uniformly across all vegetated classes, including cropland, rather than switching cropland to FAO-56 — a real, flagged simplification (no region-correct crop calendar built yet), more defensible than applying the wrong Northern-Hemisphere one. Computed per land-cover class (zonal-averaged NDVI, not per-pixel) and fed via the CSV biophysical table, not the raster-override path described above.

The test plan

Decided with Becky, 2026-09-09: test in Borneo. Every raw input the model needs is downloaded and content-verified — AOI, DEM, routing parameters, LULC, soil group, precipitation, ET0, NDVI, and the CN base (data/swy_shared_package/, ~1.1GB, ready to upload). The CN/Kc biophysical table and a placeholder rain-events table are built. A first real in-house run attempt was made 2026-09-11 via Docker, and it worked: the full standard SWY output set exists, including the final aggregated-results shapefile with a real computed baseflow value. Quickflow and actual ET both land in physically plausible ranges. Whole pipeline consolidated into real, reproducible scripts: Python_scripts/swy_borneo_run/ (see that directory’s own README for the exact pipeline and known compromises in this run). Rich has everything needed — data and scripts both — to pick this up or extend it with his own tooling; see “Findings for Rich” below for concrete, reproducible issues found in inspring’s own packaging along the way.

The run outcome, plainly: quickflow mean 406.8mm/year (range 2.3–4837.2mm), actual ET mean 1288.0mm/year — both physically reasonable for tropical rainforest, where most rainfall infiltrates rather than running off quickly. One real, genuine issue, flagged rather than hidden: ~4.6% of local-recharge (L_sum) pixels show runaway flow-accumulation values (up to 10.9 billion, where the bulk of the distribution sits in the thousands) — the classic signature of an unresolved DEM sink or pit-fill issue, not random corruption (the rest of the raster is fine). Worth investigating before trusting L_sum-derived outputs, including the aggregated baseflow figure, quantitatively. A Docker crash (the laptop sleeping mid-run killed Docker Desktop’s backend) initially looked like a run failure — the actual output files on disk tell a different, better story, confirmed by directly reading and sanity-checking them, not by trusting the process exit code alone.

Two things worth being explicit about, since they’re a real shift from where this research started, not a detail:

  • The mangrove/flooded-savannas CN gap is not a blocker for her. Resolving that patch before testing was this project’s own caution, not a condition she set.
  • Rigorous validation against a published result isn’t the priority she cares about here either — testing that the pipeline actually runs on a real basin matters more right now than proving numerical agreement with an external benchmark.

Kept for reference, not as a current requirement: the original plan was to test against one of Hamel et al. (2020)’s own basins (Peru or Myanmar) specifically because they have published, granular output to check a result against — Peru’s CN came from an existing calibrated SWAT model (Uribe et al. 2013), Myanmar’s from Mandle et al. (2017) (Hamel co-authored both — one small research lineage, not independent sources). That reasoning is still scientifically sound and worth returning to if a rigor-focused validation is wanted later; it just isn’t what this round is for.

First run output — interactive preview

Annual quickflow (QF), mm: 9.4 – 4837.2 mm
Actual evapotranspiration (AET), mm: -0.0 – 1566.0 mm
Local recharge sum (L_sum), mm — capped at p99 to show the real anomaly: -29059.8 – 26768076.5 mm
Viridis colormap. L_sum is capped at its 99th percentile so the real spatial signal stays visible against the ~4.6% of pixels with runaway flow-accumulation values (see the write-up above) — those pixels render as the brightest yellow. Toggle layers with the control in the top right; drag/scroll to pan and zoom.

Findings for Rich, from actually trying to build inspring in Docker

Concrete and reproducible, not “it didn’t work”:

  1. inspring’s own Dockerfile fails immediately on pip3 install -r requirements.txt — that file was deleted from the repo in 2022 and never replaced. Confirmed by actually running the build, not just reading the file.
  2. setup.py’s packages list omits inspring.seasonal_water_yield — a normal pip install . compiles the Cython extension but the Python module itself isn’t importable afterward. Worked around (not fixed upstream) via python setup.py build_ext --inplace + PYTHONPATH pointed at the source tree directly.
  3. Good news: the current upstream ecoshard (not the old pinned therealspring/ecoshard@b9b4580 fork commit) works fine — its bundled ecoshard.geoprocessing (with routing) and ecoshard.taskgraph have the API inspring expects. Resolves an earlier open question about whether the old fork was still required — it isn’t.
  4. This project’s own existing Docker image (therealspring/global_ncp-computational-environment) already had everything inspring actually needs — building on top of that, rather than debugging inspring’s own broken Dockerfile, is what actually worked.

Items 1 and 2 are small, well-scoped, non-scientific fixes — real candidates for a short PR back to springinnovate/inspring, not yet attempted.
